paragraphs.notes: The final B03-L1 wording is confirmed in the AFTER: 'among people of a foreign tongue.' Butler's 'of an alien speech' is a dead construction, and 'alien' now suggests extraterrestrials. 'of a foreign tongue' is Butler's own phrase for the same Greek word: 1.13 'men of a foreign tongue' renders Od. 1.183 ἐπ᾽ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους, and 3.302 has κατ᾽ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους. So this is a D29 restoration, and the edition now renders ἀλλόθροος one way. It mirrors 1.13 exactly while keeping Butler's 'people', and the final period is kept. B03-03 ('Here Zeus divided his fleet') and B03-04 ('much gold and wealth') are unchanged since R1, and this check agrees with R1's clean verdict. Zeus is the agent at Od. 3.291, 'his' still binds to Menelaus, and 'wealth' stays distinct from Butler's 'treasure' at the paragraph's end. Butler 3.23 has no 'foreign', 'tongue' or 'wealth', so there is no collision.

The revert is confirmed. B05-06 is absent from the final list, and the AFTER reads 'As he spoke, a sea broke over him', identical to the BEFORE there. The only difference in the paragraph is B05-07, 'both sail and yardarm went over'. 'yard' (the spar) reads today as a garden or a unit of length. 'yardarm' is Butler's own word for the same spar at 5.19 ('a mast with a yard arm'; AFTER 'a mast with a yardarm'), Homer's ἐπίκριον at 5.254 and 5.318. So this is D29, with one rendering for one spar, closed up per D15. No collision.

Kin sense: yes. Od. 1.49 δυσμόρῳ, ὃς δὴ δηθὰ φίλων ἄπο πήματα πάσχει ('who has long been suffering woes far from his dear ones') is the same half-line as 7.152 ἐπεὶ δὴ δηθὰ φίλων ἄπο πήματα πάσχω, which is 7.12 here and already reads 'away from my loved ones' (B07-03). Athena means Odysseus held from his own people at home, while Calypso tries 'to make him forget his home'. 'loved ones' fits: it is the literal sense of φίλοι and current and register-neutral in Athena's appeal to Zeus. Butler's 'all' and 'poor man' are kept, and so is the comma. Neither Butler 1.4 nor the AFTER has 'love' or 'dear', so there is no collision. With this edit all eight formula sites agree.
